analysis.one_liner: Bans manipulative app designs, hidden advertising, and addictive algorithms on platforms aimed at children.
analysis.headline: The KIDS Act, which would have barred autoplay, engagement-nudging features, and disguised ads on platforms used by children under 16, never received a committee vote and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have banned commercial websites and apps from using design tricks aimed at keeping children under 16 hooked — autoplay, push alerts, engagement badges, and one-tap spending — and from amplifying harmful or heavily commercial content to them through algorithms. It also would have banned influencer marketing, product placement, and other disguised advertising on child-directed platforms, ordered the FTC to audit the 25 largest child-directed platforms, and funded grants for ad-free educational content. The bill was referred to a House subcommittee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Children under 16 and their parents. Kids would face fewer features engineered to maximize their screen time and spending, less algorithmic amplification of violent, sexual, or purely commercial content, and clearer labeling of what is an ad and what is not. Parents would benefit from FTC audits of the biggest child-directed platforms, a public record of what those platforms serve children, and state attorneys general gaining power to sue violators. Nonprofit and educational creators would gain a new federal grant program (authorized at $4–12 million a year) to make ad-free content for kids.

how_it_helps.text: Bans the engagement-maximizing design features documented in the bill's own findings as manipulative of children: autoplay that chains videos without input, alerts that pull a child back to the app, public display of likes and feedback, streak-style badges for heavy use, and interfaces that push kids toward spending money or sharing personal information without parental notification.

Makes it unlawful for a platform to run algorithms that amplify sexual material, violence, self-harm, bullying, illegal activities, or wholly commercial content disguised as entertainment to users the operator knows or should know are under 16, and requires a reporting mechanism for violations.

Prohibits influencer marketing, host-selling, program-length commercials, product placement, and alcohol or nicotine marketing on child-directed platforms, and requires the FTC to write rules forcing platforms to visually distinguish commercial content from noncommercial content so children can tell advertising from entertainment.

Blocks platforms from reusing children's age-verification data for commercial purposes, directs the FTC to audit the 25 child-directed platforms with the most young users and report compliance to Congress annually, and lets state attorneys general sue violators in addition to FTC enforcement.

Creates a Commerce Department grant program, authorized at $4 million rising to $12 million a year, to fund the creation and promotion of advertisement-free, educational online content for children, with criteria set by an advisory council of child development and media experts.

analysis.who_pays: Commercial online platforms, video services, and app developers would bear the compliance cost of redesigning products and proving they know their users' ages, and would lose the engagement and ad revenue those designs produce — the digital advertising, influencer marketing, and ad-supported video industries would lose channels for reaching children. Taxpayers would fund the grant program and the FTC's rulemaking, audits, and studies. Some compliance costs would likely be passed to advertisers and, indirectly, to consumers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Online platforms, digital advertisers, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Enforcement turns on the FTC defining vague terms like content that 'unfairly encourages' a child to spend more time or money, and 'constructive knowledge' of a user's age sweeps in platforms that merely estimate or infer age — definitions broad enough to reach general-audience sites and to burden small platforms and startups with compliance costs, not just the large services the bill's findings target.

The bill restricts what algorithms may recommend and what kinds of advertising (influencer posts, product placement) may appear even to general-audience platforms once an operator has 'constructive knowledge' a user is under 16, which raises genuine commercial-speech questions and is hard to administer without collecting more age data — the very data the bill says must not be used commercially.

Implementation depends on slow FTC rulemaking: the Commission must write rules within a year, define 'program-length advertisement' by regulation, build a labeling system via a report, and run audits, so benefits would have taken years to reach families even if the bill had become law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for children — fewer addictive design loops, less disguised advertising, less algorithmic amplification of harmful content, and real FTC oversight of the biggest child-directed platforms — are substantial and directly address harms the bill documents in its findings. The costs are real but ordinary for consumer-protection regulation: compliance burdens on platforms, some definitional overbreadth that could sweep in small sites, and slow rulemaking. The strongest good-faith objection is that age-gating at 16 across general-audience platforms is difficult to do without collecting more personal data; the bill's answer — banning commercial reuse of age-verification data — is a partial fix. On balance the design is workable, though imperfect.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to a House subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Kathy Castor introduced the KIDS Act on September 30, 2021, with Reps. Yvette Clarke, Jennifer Wexton, and Lori Trahan as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day of introduction and to its Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce the next day — its last recorded action.
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or further action was ever recorded, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commercial online platforms, video services, and the digital advertising and influencer marketing industries are better off: none of the design restrictions, ad bans, or audits took effect, so engagement-driven revenue from young users continued untouched.

for.name: Rep. Kathy Castor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 10 cosponsors, all Democrats.

for.name: Reps. Yvette Clarke, Jennifer Wexton, and Lori Trahan
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on October 1, 2021 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; no action was recorded for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Technology industry and digital advertising interests
against.what_they_did: Lobbied during this period against children's online design and advertising regulation, which would have restricted engagement-driven design and ad targeting of young users.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; all 10 cosponsors were House Democrats, and the bill died in a committee controlled by the same party, so no position is on record for Republicans or most Democrats.

industries.industry: Social media and online video platforms
industries.note: The bill bans the autoplay, notification, streak-badge, and spending-nudge features these platforms use to maximize young users' time on the service, and requires public content records and annual FTC audits for the 25 largest child-directed platforms. Their engagement-based ad revenue from users under 16 was the direct target.

industries.industry: Digital advertising, ad tech, and influencer marketing
industries.note: The bill prohibits influencer marketing, host-selling, program-length commercials, and product placement on child-directed platforms, and outlaws algorithms that serve disguised commercial content to children — closing channels built specifically to reach young audiences.
The bill authorizes a federal grant program, rising to $12 million a year, to fund the creation and promotion of advertisement-free educational videos and apps for children.
